prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of Treasure Island Communications (TIC), a telecommunications company on Treasure Island which has enjoyed a government-protected monopoly for many years. TIC provides mobile services as well as fixed-line services for both international and domestic lines. In a year's time, the government will deregulate the industry and invite other companies to enter the Treasure Island market. Our client has engaged McKinsey to discuss ways to deal with this new environment.
prompt.question: Our client would like help in drawing up some possible scenarios. What information would you need in order to flesh out realistic scenarios?

clarifying_info.q: What are the government's motivations for deregulating this industry?
clarifying_info.a: Two reasons: (1) The government will collect more revenues in the form of spectrum licensing fees, and (2) Allowing more competition will reduce prices, which is better for consumers.

clarifying_info.q: What financial information is available on TIC?
clarifying_info.a: For international fixed-line services: Latest revenue = $90M; Total Costs = $30M (all annual fixed costs).

exhibits.title: International Fixed Lines — Historical Usage and Revenue
exhibits.shows: A table of historical data for TIC's international fixed-line segment showing annual revenues and total user minutes from 2006 to 2009.

framework: Market Size / Structure: Assess market size and customer base to determine whether it will remain a natural monopoly, evolve into a duopoly, oligopoly, or monopolistic competition
Characteristics of Potential Competitors: Identify capabilities of likely entrants and which segments (mobile, domestic/international fixed) they will target
Entry Barriers: Evaluate natural barriers (high setup costs, high fixed costs) and artificial barriers TIC can create (e.g., lobbying for higher spectrum-licensing fees)

Financial Analysis of TIC: Understand revenue (pricing, volumes, trends) and cost structure (setup costs, recurring fixed costs, variable costs) across segments to model break-even scenarios under competition

questions.prompt: Part 1 (Simplified): Assume prices drop 50% due to competition but usage volumes do NOT change. What market share does TIC need to maintain to break even on international fixed-line services?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute the new total market revenue at the lower price, then divide TIC's fixed costs by that figure. Should note that TIC currently holds 100% market share and can afford to lose no more than 1/3 of it.

math.setup: New market revenue = 50% × $90M = $45M. TIC break-even revenue = total fixed costs = $30M. Required market share = break-even revenue / new market revenue.
steps: TIC currently holds 100% share, so it can lose at most 1/3 of the market
math.answer: TIC needs to retain at least 2/3 (≈67%) market share to break even.

questions.prompt: Part 2 (Realistic): Using the historical data in Exhibit 1, derive historical prices and the price-volume relationship, then calculate the new market size at $0.50/min and TIC's required market share to break even.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate implied price per minute each year (revenue / minutes), identify the pattern that each time price halves volume increases 50%, project volume at $0.50, compute new market revenue, and divide fixed costs by it. Key insight: rising volumes mean break-even share is lower than in the simplified scenario.

math.setup: Price = Revenue / Total User Minutes for each year. Identify demand pattern, then project at $0.50/min. New market revenue = $0.50 × projected minutes. Required share = $30M / new market revenue.
steps: Pattern: each time price halves, volume increases 50%
math.answer: TIC needs to retain approximately 44% market share to break even — significantly lower than the 67% in the simplified scenario, because rising volumes expand the market.

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential scenarios and strategic responses TIC should prepare for as the market deregulates?

categories.name: Market Structure Scenarios
ideas: Remain near-monopoly if entry barriers stay high (e.g., high spectrum fees)
Duopoly with one major entrant targeting the most profitable segment (international fixed)
Oligopoly with multiple entrants across mobile and fixed segments
Rapid price war driving margins to near zero across all segments

categories.name: Competitive Entry Barriers TIC Can Leverage
ideas: Lobby government to set high spectrum-licensing fees that deter entry
Accelerate network investment to widen infrastructure gap
Lock in enterprise and government customers with long-term contracts
Build brand loyalty programs for consumer segments

categories.name: Strategic Responses
ideas: Aggressive price reduction pre-emptively to reduce entrant appeal
Bundle mobile and fixed-line offerings to increase switching costs
Seek regulatory advantages or exclusivity in rural/underserved areas
Explore acquisitions or partnerships with likely entrants

recommendation: No formal recommendation was requested in this case; the focus is on scenario analysis and break-even math

If pressed: TIC must retain at least 44% of the international fixed-line market (under realistic demand elasticity assumptions) and should proactively explore entry barriers, product bundling, and pricing strategy across all segments before deregulation occurs
risks: Entrants may target the most profitable segments first (international fixed), eroding TIC's best margins
Regulatory lobbying may fail, resulting in low spectrum fees and easy entry
Demand elasticity may be even higher than historical data suggests, shrinking required share further but also reducing per-unit profitability
Mobile segment dynamics (not modeled here) may be even more competitive
next_steps: Conduct same break-even analysis for mobile and domestic fixed-line segments
Model 2–3 competitor entry scenarios with different market share outcomes
Assess feasibility and cost of erecting entry barriers
Develop a lobbying and regulatory strategy ahead of deregulation deadline
